extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, IP lawyers, and policymakers involved in assessing novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining what counts as prior art and how disclosures affect novelty and inventive step (including treatment of electronic/new media, pending applications, timing, place, confidentiality, burden of proof, and doctrinal tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art on novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure can cause loss of novelty and/or inventive step (i.e., an invention may be denied novelty and inventive step by prior art disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions treat the effects on novelty and inventive step similarly (e.g., Portugal: 'the effect ... is the loss of novelty and inventive step'). Certain statutory provisions (e.g., Singapore Sections 13–15) separate novelty, inventive step and sufficiency and specify which materials form the state of the art for each requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending (earlier) patent applications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending applications of earlier priority may be considered prior art for novelty (in some laws) but are often excluded from inventive step assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Poland — pending applications of earlier priority not yet available to the public are considered prior art in assessment of novelty provided they will be published, but are not taken into account in assessment of the inventive step; Korea — pending unpublished applications affect only novelty; Singapore — Section 14(3) makes certain published patent applications part of the state of the art for novelty but excludes them for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prior art / state of the art (enabling disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art comprises everything made available to the public before the priority date by description, by use or by any other means, in such a way as to be understood and worked by those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portugal and other reports quote definitions requiring that disclosure be 'understood and worked by those skilled in the art'. Singapore emphasizes that for novelty the disclosure must be enabling — enabling a skilled person to make a product or operate a process applying common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means/forms of disclosure — breadth of recognized media
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no limitations on means of disclosure: printed publications, electronic documents, oral disclosure, disclosure by use, invoices, manuals, certificates, exhibitions, etc., may all constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland: 'not only printed publications ... also disclosure in any other form, including proofs of the open use ... (invoices, service manuals, certificates, etc)'. Korea: recognizes publications, electronic documents accessible through electric communication lines, and oral disclosure or disclosure by use. Romania/Portugal/Singapore likewise treat many forms as capable of constituting disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure through new media / internet is sufficient if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless information on electronic networks (internet, WWW) constitutes sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step if it is accessible by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korea: includes the Worldwide Web but excludes private chat groups/forums/email; Portugal and Romania consider internet disclosures sufficient provided a date of issuing/accessibility can be identified. Singapore treats internet material as part of the state of the art if made available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encrypted, password-protected or paywalled material
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted or otherwise non-public information generally does not constitute disclosure; passwords, search engines and payment requirements may affect accessibility but are not always determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland/Romania/Korea indicate encrypted/secret information may not destroy novelty. Portugal and Korea state that encryption/password/payment are not necessarily relevant or that encrypted information may be excluded. Jurisdictions differ; courts/legislation may require actual public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure (geographical relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place of disclosure is generally irrelevant for written/electronic disclosures (disclosure anywhere in the world can form prior art); place can be relevant for disclosure by use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland: 'place of the disclosure is irrelevant' (even obscure library items count). Portugal/Romania/Singapore: disclosure anywhere in Portugal or elsewhere / worldwide counts. Korea: place relevant for disclosure by use only; for written/electronic documents place is determined by distribution or place of access but is not generally relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of disclosure — no temporal cutoff except before priority date (with limited exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any disclosure made before the priority date is relevant; there are generally no limits beyond which an earlier publication ceases to be prior art, with statutory exceptions/grace periods in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland/Portugal/Korea/Singapore state no general time limits beyond the priority date. Romania provides a specific 12‑month exception where disclosures by the inventor (or successor) within 12 months preceding filing may be disregarded; Korea and others recognize limited six-month grace periods in certain circumstances (e.g., accidental disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof regarding internet or other disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof that a specific piece of information was disclosed (e.g., on the internet) lies with the person asserting the disclosure; in some reports burden falls on the party seeking to invalidate/grant based on the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland: 'The burden of proof should be on the part objecting the granting ... on the ground of lacking novelty.' Portugal/Korea/Singapore: opinions that burden lies on the party asserting the disclosure; Korea explicitly: 'A person or persons who will benefit from the fact of the disclosure ... shall have the burden of proof.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Who disclosed / good or bad faith is irrelevant (except grace/confidentiality rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally it does not matter who made the disclosure or whether made in good or bad faith; the mere fact of public disclosure counts, except where confidentiality or statutory grace periods apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland and Singapore: who made disclosure and the discloser's intent are irrelevant. Several jurisdictions (Romania, Korea) provide exceptions where disclosures by inventor or disclosures made in breach of confidentiality may be disregarded if certain conditions (e.g., notification, 6–12 month filing) are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of confidentiality / disclosures by persons under confidentiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made by persons bound by confidentiality agreements may be treated as not being public disclosures in certain circumstances (often coupled with a grace period if applicant files within a statutory period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korea: if disclosure by a person bound by confidentiality, and application filed within six months, novelty assessed without that disclosure. Romania: similar carve-out for disclosures by inventor or successor in title within 12 months preceding filing; notifications required. No uniform approach across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient's ability to understand — enabling standard / reverse engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure must be made in such a way as to be understood and worked by those skilled in the art; the mere possibility of obtaining the information through additional difficult steps (reverse engineering/disassembly) may be insufficient if it requires effort beyond that of the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portugal and Romania require that disclosure be 'understood and worked by those skilled in the art'. Korea notes that if third parties can recognize the invention only through additional steps with technical difficulties beyond what a skilled person could easily conceive, it does not constitute a relevant disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaicing (combining multiple prior art pieces) — novelty vs inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty, prior art is generally read document-by-document (no 'mosaicing'); inventive step assessment may involve combining teachings from multiple prior art documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romania: Rule 32A — for novelty, documents are taken individually (not opposable in mosaic system). Poland notes that if different technical features are disclosed in different publications but a skilled person could combine them to achieve the same result, this affects inventive step (lack of inventive step rather than novelty). Singapore cites case law disallowing mosaicing for novelty except where documents refer to each other or form a series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment test — inevitability / clear and unmistakeable directions
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine anticipation, compare the earlier disclosure with the patent claim as at its publication date; if the prior art so construed discloses the same product/process or contains 'clear and unmistakeable directions' to the invention, the claim is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singapore cites General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone: both prior art and claim must be interpreted at date of publication without hindsight. The practical question: does following the teachings in that disclosure inevitably lead to the invention?

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment — Windsurfing (four-step) approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess inventive step by: (a) identifying the inventive concept; (b) assuming the notional skilled but unimaginative addressee and imputing common general knowledge; (c) identifying differences between prior art and invention; (d) asking whether those differences would have been obvious without hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singapore follows the Windsurfing International v Tabur Marine approach; many reports adopt this structured analysis to avoid hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional inventive-step indicia — 'well‑worth‑trying' and 'lying on the road' tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may apply supplementary tests: the 'well‑worth‑trying' test (invention obvious if skilled person would have felt it was well worth trying) and the 'lying on the road' test (obvious if prior art was readily available to research workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singapore reports recent case law applying these tests alongside Windsurfing to determine obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant procedural obligations — citing closest prior art and priority allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may be required to present known prior art useful for understanding the invention, cite documents, and show at least one closest solution; when claiming priority an applicant may be obliged to allocate one and only one priority date per claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romania: Rule 13 requires presentation of prior art known to applicant and identification of the closest solution; Poland: 'claiming priority, the Applicant is obliged to point out (allocate) one and only one priority date for each claim.' These are procedural duties that affect examination clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of withdrawn/abandoned/unpublished applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications that were withdrawn, abandoned or rejected prior to publication are not considered part of the prior art in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romania: if an application is withdrawn/abandoned/rejected prior to its publication, this is not considered to belong to the prior art. Other jurisdictions may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic disclosure — place of disclosure is place of accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For internet postings, the place of disclosure is treated as the place(s) where the information can be accessed; mere availability on a website is sufficient for disclosure in the accessing location(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portugal/Korea/Romania assert that the place of disclosure for internet material is the place where it can be accessed; Korea: 'a mere fact that a paperless information is obtainable on a web-site is sufficient for a disclosure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/duration and archives for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally no formal timing/duration requirements for electronic disclosures, though some groups recommend archives or that the information be accessible for a sufficient period for a skilled person to apprehend the teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korea: no formal timing requirements but information should have been accessible long enough for a skilled person; Romania: 'archives are necessary' for electronic means (opinion). Practices differ and some reports call for archiving standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and concerns for internet-sourced evidence (manipulation / proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential manipulation of internet information and identifying proof of disclosure raise evidentiary concerns; some groups call for different standards/rules for recognition of such disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Korea/Romania note absence of settled rules and express need for discussion/harmonisation: who bears burden of proof, how to deal with manipulation, and what accessibility levels suffice. Portugal and others opine Internet does not require different rules, while Romania/Korea recommend specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute novelty approach (policy stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some groups endorse 'absolute' novelty: any public disclosure anywhere, by any means, before the priority date destroys novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland: group opinion that 'absolute' novelty has to be applied, irrespective of time, place and way in which invention has been disclosed. Several reports stress broad definitions of prior art similar to EPC practice.
